title: IXOPAY Launches IXO One, a Modular Payments Platform Built for Agentic Commerce
snippet: IXOPAY has unveiled IXO One, a modular, AI-native payments platform combining orchestration, tokenisation and payments intelligence, with agentic payment capabilities and general availability planned for early 2027. The post IXOPAY Launches IXO One, a Modular Payments Platform Built for Agentic Commerce appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Payment infrastructure provider IXOPAY has unveiled IXO One, a modular, AI-native platform that brings its orchestration, tokenisation and payments intelligence products together in one place. The pitch to merchants is flexibility: buy the components they need, build the ones that set them apart, and swap providers without tearing up the whole payment stack. General availability of the first unified experience is planned for early 2027.

One platform, three products

Merchants selling across channels, countries and payment methods often end up running a patchwork of acquirers, processors and gateways. Adding a new payment method or market can mean a heavy integration project, and moving away from a provider can mean rebuilding large parts of the stack. Dallas-based IXOPAY is positioning IXO One as the answer to that problem, describing it as the first modular, AI-native payments platform to combine orchestration, payments intelligence and tokenisation in a single offering.

The platform pulls IXOPAY’s existing products under one portal with a common developer experience. Merchants can take ready-made capabilities off the shelf, build their own where it matters, and keep

ownership of their payment service provider connections through an Adapter SDK. Components can be added or removed later, and providers changed, without a full rebuild. IXOPAY says the aim is to cut

provider dependency, costly migrations and the technical debt that builds up when payment stacks are bolted together over time.

Also included is IXO AI, an assistant that lets merchants query their payment data in plain language, see what needs attention and act on what they find

Built for AI agents that pay

Ajoy Krishnamoorthy, CEO at Ixopay

The more forward-looking part of the launch is the Agentic Suite, which prepares merchants for purchases started by AI agents rather than people. It has three parts. A Payment Agent connects merchant-owned shopping agents, IXOPAY-powered experiences and supported third-party agents through a single integration, rather than one per protocol. Universal Tokens let payment data be stored and used across providers and buying experiences without exposing raw card credentials to an agent, with records of the agent’s identity, the customer’s consent and the purchase intent kept to support traceability and disputes. An MCP Server lets approved AI assistants carry out authorised payment and tokenisation tasks, checking existing user permissions, limiting access to authorised vaults, keeping API credentials away from the AI client and logging each action for audit.

IXOPAY chief executive Ajoy Krishnamoorthy frames the launch around buyers who now move between channels, payment methods and countries faster than most payment stacks can follow.

Demand for composable payments

Analysts see the same shift. 451 Research, part of S&P Global, points to payments becoming a boardroom priority, to multi-processor set-ups becoming common, and to merchants wanting to plug into newer commerce frameworks such as agentic commerce and accelerated guest checkout. Its view is that providers should prioritise modular and composable offerings to meet that demand.

Phased roll-out

IXO One will roll out in phases, with general availability of the first unified experience and a new, flexible commercial model planned for early 2027. In the meantime, new and existing customers can continue to buy IXOPAY’s orchestration, tokenisation and payments intelligence products individually, along with its connector network and integration services.

IXOPAY says its orchestration platform recorded an 80 per cent year-on-year rise in transaction count to October 2026 and has supported more than USD 200 billion in payment volume since 2018. It connects merchants to more than 200 payment service providers and 300 payment methods.

title: The Future of Global Payments Is an Operating System
snippet: PhotonPay CEO Lewison Chen outlines why global payments need an operating system to unify fiat and stablecoins, backed by a $40M Series C to scale multi-rail money movement. The post The Future of Global Payments Is an Operating System appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
While modern enterprises run front-office sales on sophisticated SaaS platforms, automate workflows with artificial intelligence, and manage supply chains via real-time ERPs, cross-border treasury management remains anchored in legacy friction. According to Lewison Chen, founder and chief executive officer of global fintech PhotonPay, the fundamental bottleneck in B2B payments is no longer a lack of payment rails, digital wallets, or regional bank accounts, but the absence of a unified financial operating system.

Lewison Chen, founder & CEO at PhotonPay

Chen’s analysis arrives as PhotonPay closes a $40 million Series C funding round led by Blockchain Capital, with participation from Japanese financial giant SBI Group alongside existing investors IDG Capital, GL Ventures, and Lightspeed Faction. The capital injection is directly earmarked to scale PhotonPay’s stablecoin-centric Financial Operating System (Financial OS)—an infrastructure layer engineered to orchestrate fiat clearing, foreign exchange, card issuing, and digital asset settlement into a single, automated architecture.

Abstracting Complexity: The Operating System Paradigm

Historically, the cross-border payments sector has prioritized connectivity: linking more domestic clearing houses, onboarding regional banks, and supporting local alternative payment methods. However, Chen argues that sheer network expansion has created severe operational fragmentation for cross-border businesses, which must still navigate disjointed compliance regimes, disparate cut-off times, and multi-portal reconciliations.

Drawing a parallel to the evolution of personal computing, Chen notes that platforms such as Windows and macOS unlocked mainstream utility not by educating users on microprocessors, but by abstracting hardware complexities behind an intuitive graphical interface. Global money movement requires an identical architectural transition:

“The next generation of financial infrastructure must answer a different question: How do we make all that complexity manageable without making businesses navigate it themselves? A true Financial OS needs to connect to bank accounts, local clearing systems, card networks, foreign exchange infrastructure, and emerging stablecoin rails, while abstracting their different rules, formats, settlement windows, and liquidity requirements into one unified infrastructure layer.”

Under this model, commercial enterprises express only high-level commercial intent—the origin, destination, volume, and settlement deadline—while the operating system determines the optimal routing rail behind the scenes.

Rejecting the Binary: Bridging Fiat and Stablecoins

Chen dismisses the prevailing industry debate that positions fiat rails and blockchain-based stablecoins as mutually exclusive competitors. For institutional and B2B commerce, fiat infrastructure remains the foundational anchor for payroll, supplier payments, tax compliance, and local commerce.

However, because traditional banking rails remain constrained by business-day clearing cut-offs and regional operating hours, stablecoins provide a continuous, 24/7 value-transfer mechanism. The real breakthrough lies in multi-rail orchestration rather than forcing businesses to manually bridge digital assets:

“If a customer still has to decide when to use a bank network, when to acquire stablecoins, and when to convert back into fiat, we have not actually reduced complexity. We have simply added another layer of it. The value of an operating system lies in orchestration… The customer should not have to choose the rail. The system should.”

By utilizing stablecoins as an intermediate transfer mechanism—converting local fiat to digital tokens for cross-border transit, and settling back into destination fiat—enterprises gain the speed of public blockchains while preserving familiar fiat treasury workflows.

Programmable Treasury and Institutional Scale

A key component of the Financial OS is transforming treasury management from manual operational tasks into programmable software. Through direct API integration with enterprise ERPs and SaaS platforms, financial actions execute automatically based on business logic—rebalancing liquidity when regional thresholds drop, releasing supplier escrow upon milestone completions, and continuously feeding reconciliation data into accounting systems.

Founded in Hong Kong in 2015, PhotonPay has established an expansive regulatory and physical footprint to underpin this infrastructure layer:

Regulatory Footprint: Holds 34 financial and payment licenses across Asia, Europe, and the Americas.

Commercial Reach: Powers cross-border payment operations for more than 200,000 businesses across 200 countries and territories.

Global Operations: Operates 16 corporate offices worldwide supported by a workforce of nearly 600 employees.

As international commerce enters a new era defined by rapid market entry and automated software agents, Chen maintains that financial infrastructure must become largely invisible to the end user. By combining deep regulatory licensing with multi-rail fiat and stablecoin orchestration, PhotonPay is positioning its Financial OS as the foundational software engine for modern global trade.

title: Dubai FinTech Summit day one: corridors, stablecoins and a tenfold bet on talent
snippet: Dubai Future Finance Week opened on Monday at Madinat Jumeirah, with the Dubai Fintech Summit as its anchor. The first edition of the week has already outgrown its plans: more than 100 events, 12 signature forums and 14 stages across the city, and over 1,000 speakers under the theme Finance Reimagined. The post Dubai FinTech Summit day one: corridors, stablecoins and a tenfold bet on talent appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Dubai Future Finance Week opened with DIFC growing its academy tenfold, J.P. Morgan opening a private bank branch in the centre and the UAE central bank setting out how dirham stablecoins and a digital dirham will sit side by side. On stage, the argument of the day was corridors.

Dubai Future Finance Week opened on Monday at Madinat Jumeirah, with the Dubai Fintech Summit as its anchor. The first edition of the week has already outgrown its plans: more than 100 events, 12 signature forums and 14 stages across the city, and over 1,000 speakers under the theme Finance Reimagined.

A bigger bet on people

His Excellency Essa Kazim, Governor of DIFC, opened the summit by setting Dubai’s rise against what it still wants. “In little more than two decades, Dubai has become a top 10 financial centre, showing what ambition and decisive action can achieve,” he said.

The numbers he brought were about momentum. DIFC recorded more than 2,200 new active companies in the first nine months of 2026, an all-time high and 26 per cent more than a year earlier, and its AI, fintech and innovation community grew by close to 500 firms net over the past 12 months. AI, tokenisation and digital infrastructure, he argued, are not simply improving existing processes but changing the economics of financial services.

The announcement that went with it was about talent rather than towers. DIFC Academy will grow tenfold to 370,000 sq ft in the new Zabeel District, moving from three floors to a campus of three buildings with 54 seminar rooms, five research spaces and its own graduation hall. From 2030 it will be able to take more than 50,000 learners a year, against 51,620 graduates across its first two decades. His Excellency Arif Amiri, chief executive of DIFC Authority, called it an investment in the people who will shape the next generation of finance from Dubai.

The backdrop is a ranking DIFC will be quoting all week. In September’s Global Financial Centres Index, industry professionals put Dubai first in the world for fintech.

The corridor case, made by a Singapore bank

Corridors ran through the plenary programme, from a chief executives’ panel with Mambu, Network International, SC Ventures and Van Lanschot Kempen to a line-up of ministers. India’s Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman was among the day’s government speakers, alongside His Excellency Abdulla bin Touq Al Marri, the UAE’s Minister of Economy and Tourism, and His Excellency Mohamed Hassan Alsuwaidi, Minister of Investment.

The clearest statement of the case came from Jason Moo, chief executive of Bank of Singapore. As the world splits between the US and China, clients want neutral ground for their money, and Singapore and Dubai are becoming the safe harbours they choose. He does not see the two cities as rivals. Bank of Singapore runs its business from three hubs, Singapore, Hong Kong and Dubai, and he sees capital moving both ways between them. The bank has taken Chinese investors and senior managers of Chinese financial institutions to Dubai on two or three trips as they look to diversify, while Gulf clients are moving assets to Asia for safekeeping and looking to ASEAN for growth.

“I’m fully convinced around the Asian and the Middle Eastern corridor because I really feel like that’s where the next alliances will be built,” he said.

Moo also gave the day one of its more practical AI numbers. Bank of Singapore’s own AI agents now carry out KYC work, cutting account opening from around six weeks to 15 days. His warning was about what clients build for themselves. A family office that pulls bank data into a home-made dashboard without serious cyber security becomes the weakest link in the chain, which is why the bank is looking at giving clients a sandbox inside its own firewalls.

Private wealth keeps arriving

Wealth was the day’s other strand. J.P. Morgan Private Bank has opened a new branch in DIFC, regulated by the DFSA, giving it a dedicated platform to serve clients across the UAE and the wider region. The firm has used DIFC as its regional base for corporate and investment banking for 20 years, and more than tripled its Dubai private banking team over the past 12 months to be ready. Selim Elgen, UAE market head, and Karim Rekik, regional head for the Middle East, lead the team.

Two forms of digital dirham

On the second plenary stage, Paul Kayrouz, Chief Fintech Officer at the Central Bank of the UAE, explained how the country’s digital money is meant to fit together. The UAE issued a comprehensive, risk-based stablecoin regulation in 2024, and four banks are now licensed to issue dirham stablecoins, each with its own use case, from retail payments to cross-border flows, corporate treasury and intercompany settlement.

He does not expect those stablecoins to compete with the central bank’s digital dirham. The CBDC is sovereign money, issued and backed by the central bank, and is the natural rail for settlement between banks across borders, while bank-issued stablecoins go after retail, treasury and intercompany uses. The central bank wants to offer the options and let the market, not the regulator, decide which rail wins for which payment. Both serve a larger aim: taking the dirham beyond the UAE’s borders, with the central bank working to bring trading partners in Asia, Africa, the CIS and the wider Middle East onto its rails.

Kayrouz pointed to platforms already running under the central bank’s transformation programme, including an eKYC service that cuts opening a bank account from around 60 days to under a day, an instant payments platform and open finance. On agentic AI, he said the question is when, not whether. The central bank is deploying its own AI agents to watch how agents behave in the market, and he argued that agentic payments will only scale with a human on the loop rather than in it, backed by clear consumer mandates and a quick way to reverse a transaction.

The DFSA brought its own AI work to the summit. With Cambridge’s Digital Innovation and Regulation Initiative, it published a paper on how deployed and agentic AI changes cyber resilience, built around four questions: how fast a firm can close off serious exposure, how far its reliance on shared technology reaches, whether an AI system’s actions stay within its mandate, and whether the firm can establish what happened and restore critical operations. The regulator is clear that it is a contribution to research and international discussion, not guidance. DFSA chief executive Mark Steward and Bryan Zhang of the Cambridge initiative were due to discuss it at the summit.

The view from the merchant

Not everyone on the floor is in a hurry. Harry Gill, chairman of Pay10, which is now live in the UAE, Bahrain and Morocco and added a European licence this year, told The Fintech Times that stablecoin acceptance is on the roadmap for Pay10’s QR code payments, but only once regulation allows it. He doubts consumers will reach for it soon.

“If you already have a dirham account, for you to convert that into a stablecoin then make a payment to buy a coffee, I don’t see that happen right now,” he said. For Pay10, the priority is small merchants: instant settlement and lower costs first, with everything else built on top.

Small businesses were also the focus for Emirates NBD, which on Monday relaunched its National Digital Talent Incubator as NDTI AI, a programme to help established Emirati-owned SMEs among its customers put AI to work. DIFC Innovation Hub will support the programme’s design, with AWS and Visa as partners. Each cohort will take four or five businesses, with two cohorts a year, and use cases will be worked out with each business rather than picked from a fixed menu.

fullText:
Jessica Rusu, FCA chief data, information and intelligence officer at Bloomberg's UK Policy Series.

  

Speaker: Jessica Rusu, FCA chief data, information and intelligence officer

Event: Bloomberg UK Policy Series

Delivered: 19 October 2026

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version

Reading time: 8 minutes

Highlights

We want the UK to be at the forefront of the safe and responsible adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in financial services, supporting innovation, productivity and economic growth.

As AI evolves towards increasingly autonomous systems, firms should put consumers first, maintain clear accountability and plan for when things go wrong.

We are sharing examples of good and poor AI practice to help firms innovate responsibly, with a focus on putting consumers first, ensuring clear accountability and planning for failure.

The FCA is becoming a smarter regulator, using AI in its own work and taking forward the Mills Review through engagement, testing and action.

It’s great to be here today with you – humans.

The AI news cycle has become almost impossible to keep up with.

Like many of you, I’m reading a lot – how the race for faster AI chips is driving investment in data centres, creating both growth and risk across equity and debt markets.

Global spend on AI is expected to reach over $2.6 trillion this year.

That same acceleration is playing out across science and technology.

Last week, I visited a Quantum lab to see how AI is advancing cryptographic research.

And I’m fascinated by the way AI builders are turning to neuroscience to analyse the behaviour of agents, following the Hugging Face security incident.

After 25 years working at the intersection of data, technology and innovation, I have never found this field more exciting.

Adoption is not coming. It is here.

ChatGPT has reached over a billion active users.

Across financial services, firms are moving from experimentation to deployment. Our joint AI survey with the Bank of England, published next week, shows 86% of firms now use AI.

AI will redefine financial services. Done well, AI can increase productivity, improve competition, services and drive economic growth.

And the FCA wants the UK to be at the forefront of the safe adoption of AI in financial services.

    

            						

The Mills Review

That is why we commissioned the Mills Review, published in July, focused on how AI could reshape retail financial services by 2030.

Some developments we anticipated are already emerging, including the transition towards agentic finance, such as the launch of Meta’s Muse.

Our response to the review is not to consult, study and report progress. Our focus is testing, assurance, monitoring and surveillance: directly with industry to understand how AI systems are being deployed.

Whilst the Review focused on retail, the AI shift does not stop at the retail boundary. Across wholesale markets too, AI is accelerating how firms analyse, trade, monitor and make decisions.

We are embedding 6 of the 7 recommendations into live work immediately. Our innovation services such as the AI Lab give us direct insight into what firms are building from agent-led payments and fraud detection to consumer support.

On frontier AI security, we are working directly with banks to understand how frontier models are changing cyber defence, identifying and linking vulnerabilities and assisting with triaging, patching and recovering at greater speed. Those insights are feeding directly into our supervisory and policy response.

Firms are not bystanders in that process. The leaders will be those that deploy AI effectively, innovatively and safely.

But increasingly, AI is also changing what happens before a consumer ever reaches a regulated firm. Consumers are turning to general-purpose large language models (LLMs), like ChatGPT, Gemini and Claude, for financial information and advice, while regulated firms are beginning to integrate their services into AI platforms.

The good news – this can significantly widen access to financial tools and information. But it can also blur the boundary between regulated and unregulated activity, and the protections consumers receive.

Four in five less-experienced investors aged 18-40 have used AI to help with investing, but only 40% of consumers correctly recognise that there is no recourse if something goes wrong after acting on advice from a general-purpose AI tool. Our answer is not simply to expand our remit, but to make the existing boundary clearer.

Through InvestSmart and the FCA Firm Checker, we already help consumers understand the protections they have. But warnings may be more effective at the point where AI-generated financial information is delivered.

So we are calling on AI providers to help consumers understand the limits of financial information and advice generated by their models through clear, proportionate and consistent disclaimers.

And rather than create a new public-interest financial capability tool, as the Mills Review suggested, we will build on existing work, including IOSCO’s first TechSprint, powered by our AI Lab to help investors spot scams, verify information and challenge unreliable AI outputs.

          

            						

AI adoption: good and poor practice

Protecting consumers starts with how firms deploy AI.

Today, we are publishing good and poor practice drawn from our observations from firm testing this year, to give practical guidance and examples.

Three things stand out: consumer centricity, accountability and governance, and operational resilience.

Put the consumer first

The Consumer Duty provides an outcomes-based regulatory framework. We’ve seen firms using AI for inclusive product design, clear consumer choice, and a path to speak to a person. Good practice: one firm developed a live list of vulnerability signals that its chatbot can use to flag consumers who may need additional support to human advisers.

But we have seen poor practice too: firms developing AI tools without a clearly defined need, excluding vulnerable consumers by default, overstating capabilities, or deploying automated customer journeys without sufficient testing.

AI should improve consumer outcomes, not simply automate existing processes.

Know who is accountable

The second principle is governance, where too many firms are still under-investing.

Firms need clear accountability, risk-based controls, human oversight, escalation triggers, and senior managers personally accountable for AI systems.

We have seen good examples. One firm established an independent ethics panel to interrogate proposed AI use cases before deployment – including ownership, bias, and controls. But we have also seen firms retrofit governance after technology has already been deployed or fail to adapt monitoring as systems change.

That is the wrong way around.

Operational resilience

Third: stress-test AI systems. Plan for failure. Maintain fallback options. Understand supplier concentrations and dependencies, including reliance on a single model. A system that fails at scale disrupts the services consumers rely on. Make sure you have proper cyber insurance in place.

Overall, our good and poor practice finds that both firms and consumers benefit from well-deployed systems. Even AI deployed purely for internal efficiency passes value to consumers – through better-run firms, more competitive pricing, and faster service.

Our good and poor practice, published today, is not intended to be static guidance – we will update it as the technology evolves.

          

            						

From frontier AI to agentic finance

And the frontier is moving quickly – shifting from technology that helps us understand and decide, to technology that can increasingly act on our behalf.

Agents can search across products, manage payments and investments, and transact directly with other agents, creating a new layer of autonomous technology between institutions and their customers. With its strengths in fintech and financial services, the UK can lead this next wave.

But greater autonomy also changes the risk.

Poorly governed AI can create consumer harm, cyber vulnerabilities and operational failures, potentially at much greater speed and scale.

That is why firms need to invest now in cyber and operational resilience. Our rules already require firms to report major incidents, and that must extend to significant AI failures and near-misses. As the AI Minister has recognised, near-miss reporting for agentic AI is becoming a national security priority. It is a regulatory priority too.

It also means thinking differently about assurance. A system that is safe at deployment may behave differently at scale, under stress or as the models beneath it change. Agentic systems therefore require continuous, conditional assurance.

The FCA will work with industry, fellow regulators and frontier labs to develop a trusted framework for agentic finance, including clear approaches to agent identity, delegated authority, accountability and execution.

Our aim is to create the conditions in which agentic finance can thrive, with innovation and consumer protection built together from the start.

          

            						

Becoming an agentic regulator

And the FCA itself is changing. Part of our work to become a smarter regulator means developing our future as an agentic regulator, using the same technologies reshaping our markets to make ourselves sharper, faster, and more effective.

Across the FCA we are deploying AI to scale our operations and focus on the greatest harms, upskilling staff and investing in technology. AI can gather evidence, surface intelligence from disparate sources, and flag early warning signs so we can act at pace.

For example, we are building AI tools for the oversight of 60,000 anti-money laundering (AML) firms coming into the FCA’s remit in 2028. We are deploying automation and building AI agentic tools – like our market first responder agent – which will supervise ~9,000 small wholesale markets transaction reporting firms, so supervisors can prioritise more complex supervisory activities.

Dynamic data collection becomes part of the future of supervision. Building on our launch in August of the FCA’s Handbook API, giving access to firms to digest our machine-readable rules via their AI tools, we are also working on machine-readable data collection APIs.

And leveraging our AI Lab and Sandbox environment becomes ever more important for system-wide simulations and method of supervision.

          

            						

Conclusion

I began by saying it was good to be here among humans. While that was light-hearted, there is a serious point behind the work we must do together.

AI is moving faster than any regulatory framework was designed. That means regulators will increasingly need to make judgements without precedent, while ensuring that trust remains at the heart of financial services.

We remain focused on our strategy, becoming a smarter regulator, using technology to become faster and more effective, enabling markets that work well – for consumers, for growth, and for the long term.

Building on our world-leading approach to innovation and proportionate regulation, we believe developing the best approach to deploying AI safely is what will differentiate the UK market.

The future of finance is being built now. Let's build it together.

title: BNPL bolsters holiday budgets: survey
snippet: Younger shoppers favor buy now, pay later loans more than their older counterparts, but BNPL companies draw consumers across income brackets, a survey finds.
fullText:
An article from
        
    

        

                Dive Brief
        

                

Younger shoppers favor buy now, pay later loans more than their older counterparts, but BNPL companies draw consumers across income brackets, a survey finds.

        

            

        Published Nov. 2, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                Shoppers wait to enter a store at the Woodbury Commons premium outlets mall on Nov. 25, 2022 in Woodbury, New York.
            
        
            Getty Images
        
    
    
    

Dive Brief:

During the 2026 holiday season, a fifth of consumers said they’ll use buy now, pay later providers more than they did last year, according to a survey by the Electronic Transactions Association and TSG, The Strawhecker Group, a payments consulting firm. While a quarter said their BNPL usage will remain the same, nearly half (47%) said they don’t anticipate using BNPL payments at all.

Among people who like using BNPL services, 52% said the payment method allows them to manage large expenses, while 45% use it for unexpected purchases, the survey of 1,099 consumers found.

As for consumers who eschew BNPL options, 73% said they don’t like accruing debt, and 55% don’t want to risk paying high fees or interest payments, per the annual survey, which was released Wednesday.

Dive Insight:

The survey by the ETA and TSG — which gathered responses from U.S. consumers across genders, income levels, generations and geographic areas — suggests that consumers’ perceptions of BNPL payments vary by generation and income level. 

When asked how they felt about their BNPL purchases over the past few months, about four in ten (37%) of consumers across income levels and generations viewed BNPL services favorably, compared to 36% with an unfavorable view. 

While 47% of millennials viewed BNPL payments favorably, 39% of Gen Zers, 38% of Gen Xers and 24% of Baby Boomers said the same. Meanwhile, about a third (35%) of low-income and high-income consumers like BNPL payments, compared to 40% of middle-income consumers who prefer the payment method, the survey found. 

The survey also shed light on which new payment methods consumers have tried over the 12 months. 

At the top of the list was tap-to-pay at 53%, followed by digital wallets (31%) and peer-to-peer apps (28%). By contrast, only 9% said they had tried BNPL in the past year, and cryptocurrencies were lowest at 3% during that same period, the survey found.

The survey tracked a similar pattern from prior years for the payment methods consumers use regularly. 

Among the payment methods consumers said they used regularly, tap-to-pay ranked first at 81%, followed by digital wallets (61%) and peer-to-peer apps (60%). About a fifth (21%) of survey respondents said they used BNPL services regularly; cryptocurrency payments came in last again at only 8%, per the survey results. 

“Convenience and familiarity are converting trial into repeat behavior more effectively than novelty alone,” the report said. “Once consumers try tap-to-pay, digital wallets, and P2P apps, a large share continue using them; driving the first successful transaction remains an important adoption lever.”

Along with TSG’s and the Electronic Transactions Association’s findings, other surveys suggest that consumers perceive BNPL services as a tool for spreading out their payments. In a recent PayPal Holdings survey of 2,005 adults, about six in ten consumers reported leaning toward BNPL payments to extend their holiday budgets and control their spending.

Consumers turned to BNPL payments last year to divvy up their purchases, Block subsidiary Afterpay said earlier this year. During the 2025 holiday season, the company noted that most (96%) of its customers who used its installment payment services for Black Friday and Cyber Monday shopping had repaid their debts early or on time.

Global payments are moving faster, but local settlement remains a pain point for many companies, according to speakers on a Money20/20 panel.

        

            

        Published Oct. 29, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                An exhibition hall sign greeted attendees at the 2026 Money20/20 financial technology conference in Las Vegas.
            
        
            Justin Bachman/Payments Dive
        
    
    
    

Dive Brief:

Settlement of a cross-border payment at its destination remains a pain point across the industry, despite improvements in rails, speed and interoperability among players, payments executives said last week in a panel discussion.

The last portion of a cross-border payment accounts for 80% of the total speed of a transaction, regardless of the payment rail or instrument that is used, said Leigh Amaro, Americas CEO for Swift, the digital financial messaging firm for international payments. Amaro spoke about how cross-border payments are evolving on Oct. 20 at the Money20/20 financial technology conference in Las Vegas.

Given current regulations, “an instrument can leave one country looking like one thing and completely end up in another's jurisdiction looking completely different,” Debopama Sen, Citigroup’s head of payments and services, said during the discussion. “And then when you marry that with regulatory cross-border restriction challenges, the last mile is where our clients struggle, and the last mile does need to be addressed.”

Dive Insight:

Cross-border payments totaled about $190 trillion last year, generating about $290 billion in revenue for the payments industry, according to an August report from the consulting firm McKinsey.

Three-quarters of Swift-enabled payments reach the recipient’s beneficiary bank within 10 minutes, Amaro said. At that point, however, local rules, operating hours and other challenges slow the settlement process, regardless of whether a payment was sent via stablecoin, tokenized deposit or a traditional rail, she said.

Meanwhile, regulators in many countries are pushing for more price transparency with respect to the services, while compliance complexity has increased due to newer fintech entrants into the cross-border arena, the McKinsey report noted.

Some of the costs and complexities of cross-border payments are slowly decreasing, threatening to commoditize the field, said Jonathan Zell, a McKinsey partner in the consulting firm’s payments practice, who moderated the session.

Kush Saxena, CEO of Banking Circle Group, a Luxembourg-based fintech that specializes in cross-border payments, challenged that contention, drawing a distinction between cash and data transfers.

“I wouldn’t say moving money is a commodity. I think moving data is becoming easier,” Saxena said, noting “a ton of interoperability” the industry has created above the fiat level. “When it comes to fiat, you get into sort of regulated territory, and … there is a 180-degree divide between where global commerce is going and between where regulators are going.”

One area that Citi and other banks are working to solve is “bridging the world of blockchain and digital assets with the fiat world” in cross-border payments, Sen said. She said Citi clients have been seeking this capability “because they’re not really looking at it, saying, ‘Hey, I want to use that technology.’ They’re saying, ‘Can you solve my problem?’”

Last month, Citibank introduced a cross-border, instant-payment service, using its global network and collaborating with Swift, to help customers avoid the need for local banking relationships.

“Data can move at the speed of light, but that’s not enough. The cash has to be available,” Sen said, noting the success of the M-Pesa money-transfer service in Africa due to its abundant cash-payout locations in each country.

fullText:
Speech by Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive, at Investment Association Annual Dinner 2026.

  

Speaker: Sarah Pritchard, deputy chief executive

Event: Investment Association Annual Dinner 2026, Guildhall, City of London

Delivered: 20 October 2026

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version.

Reading time: 6 minutes

Highlights

In an ever-changing environment, our strategy is our anchor. Our priorities – supporting growth, being a smarter regulator, helping consumers and fighting financial crime – help us decide consistently and act for the long term.  

While we are past the peak of rule making, we are still taking a deliberate, strategic approach to reform rather than taking a piecemeal approach.

We encourage firms to engage with us. Tell us where the friction lies so we can build a system that works together.

Look around.

This building has stood for more than 600 years. It’s survived both the Great Fire and the Blitz. 

And yet it still endures. Because when it had to be, it was rebuilt deliberately.

That’s the lesson I want to borrow tonight.

The world around Guildhall looks nothing like it did – and neither does your industry. Technology and AI mean markets are changing faster, and more fundamentally, than ever before.

But one thing is constant. 

Markets have always been rooted in trust.

Trust is fundamental to the success of your sector.

And it is a successful sector. 

London ranks second globally in the Global Financial Centres Index, just behind New York.

And millions trust you with their savings. Their pensions. Their very futures.

Total assets under management have now reached £16.5tn – that’s nearly 5 times the UK’s GDP.

But success is no reason to stand still.  

    

            						

Reform: more than writing rules

In this sector, we’re just past peak rule making.  

The scale of change has been significant – and deliberate.

But we’re not done yet.

We want to see growth that benefits consumers, supports competitiveness and spurs innovation.

Building a stronger retail investment culture takes more than piecemeal rule writing.

It takes a strategic approach.  

One that starts with giving consumers the support they need to make informed financial decisions. 

And understand both the risks of acting – and the costs of not acting.

In that vein, we have reformed our advice and guidance rules.

We’ve introduced targeted support.

And we’ve moved away from prescriptive disclosures, and placed greater emphasis on outcomes through the Consumer Duty.

We want to further support innovation and give firms the confidence to offer more forms of simplified advice at lower cost to consumers.

So we’ll soon publish updated rules, alongside case studies we’ve developed with the Financial Ombudsman Service.

We’re already seeing real progress.

Just 6 months in, more than a dozen firms are already authorised to deliver targeted support.

And early signs are promising: consumers who receive it invest up to 53% more than those who don’t.

These reforms have taken time and effort – from your teams, and mine.

But it’s well worth it.

          

            						

Our report card

Last year we set out a new 5-year strategy.

To support growth, be a smarter regulator, help consumers navigate their financial lives and fight financial crime.

These aren’t separate goals. Each one helps us do our job of making markets work well.  

We’re pleased with the progress we’ve made so far.

Our latest Practitioner Panel survey found that three quarters of firms have high trust in us, and the same proportion support our strategy.

More than 7 in 10 agree our work enhances the UK’s reputation as a financial centre.  

And nearly 9 in 10 now understand the Consumer Duty’s requirements – a big change from last year.

But we know there’s more to do. 

Which is why we’ll stay focused on reducing burden, including by simplifying data returns.

And expand our innovation services, where applications rose 89% in the first year of our strategy.

From our Scale-up Unit to our AI sandboxes, we’re helping firms access funding, test new ideas and innovate more quickly.

And we’ll keep sharing what we learn to help firms innovate effectively. 

          

            						

Challenges ahead

Still, financial crime remains a challenge – at home and abroad.

In the UK, investment fraud losses alone rose 40% in 2025.  

And that’s despite us being ever more assertive.

We’re securing more criminal convictions than ever before across fraud, money laundering and insider dealing.

Last year, we issued over 2,300 scam and unauthorised firm warnings.

And in recent weeks, we’ve made 3 arrests as part of a major insider dealing investigation and helped the Metropolitan Police disrupt a suspected serious organised crime network.

But intervention is just part of the equation.

Regulator and industry alike have to help consumers use financial services safely.

The Investment Association has Savvy the Squirrel to help build confidence to invest.

And we have Emil the Seal to point people to our Firm Checker.

Since its launch in January, consumers have used it nearly 2 million times to make sure firms are authorised and genuine.

A partnership between Emil and Savvy could be a powerful one, especially if firms point consumers to Firm Checker. 

What is clear is that with the speed and scale of this threat, we can’t do this on our own.

This fight calls for a system-wide response – because scams undermine trust, market integrity and consumer confidence.

So work with us.

In July, we published our review of financial crime controls in asset management and alternatives.

We found good practice and room for improvement – particularly in higher-risk areas, such as private markets.

Our message is clear: tailor your financial crime controls to the risks.

Our ask is clear, too: share intelligence early. Flag the gaps in the system. And help us stop criminals exploiting them.

It’s how markets stay trusted and confident.

          

            						

Working differently to support a changing world

Change is happening at a breakneck speed.

More technology. More cross-border activity. More innovation.

All moving faster than traditional regulation can keep up with.  

Which is why we’re not just regulating for the market as it is today. We’re future-proofing it.

By setting clear, outcomes-focused standards, using better data to spot emerging risks and keeping our rules under review as markets evolve.  

That approach keeps us open-minded in the face of change. 

And our regulation and rulebook proportionate and fit for the future.  

Take the package of reforms we consulted on this summer. By streamlining the rulebook for asset managers, we could save firms £128m per year.  

Our proposed fund reporting framework is part of that: simpler reporting for firms, better data for us to consider as we review our rules and see how markets are operating.  

We’re collecting responses until Thursday, so there’s still time to have your say. 

I’ve always said we can’t regulate just for yesterday’s challenges. We have to let markets evolve.  

And we are.

We worked previously to support industry and IA-led blueprints for fund tokenisation.  

Now, we’re helping firms put them into practice.

Baillie Gifford tested the technology behind its tokenised fund in our regulatory sandbox. That fund was authorised in under a year.  

Next month, our joint tokenisation roadmap with the Bank of England will set the path from testing to lasting infrastructure for markets as a whole.  

But change also demands preparation.  

With T+1 settlement less than a year away, we are focused on this sector’s readiness.

So be prepared – because we will act if you’re not. 

After all, market integrity is at stake. 

Getting outcomes-focused regulation right means you don’t need to wait for new rules to innovate.

And this will move us beyond a cycle of constant rule making to one of us checking that our rules work as intended.

We already do this regularly.  

You’ve seen it in the removal of rules requiring a 7-day delay in initial public offerings. 

Our review of the Consumer Duty’s application to wholesale markets. 

And our Advice Guidance Boundary Review and unbundling of research rules.

You’ve also just heard me say we’re just past the peak of rule making.

While it may not feel like it yet, it will eventually – I promise!  

When it does, our focus will be clear. 

Keep what works. Fix what doesn’t. And keep growth and innovation at the centre of it.

          

            						

Becoming the regulator of the future

Being the right kind of regulator means being right for today and tomorrow.

Later this week at Mansion House, our chief executive will speak about what a changing world means for modern regulators.

The same question applies here.

There are more opportunities – for firms and criminals – than ever before. And we have to meet them differently. 

By making better use of data and technology and focusing our supervision where risk actually sits.

AI already helps us cut through large data sets to identify risks sooner and act more quickly.

We'll keep exploring where we can go from here. Because we don’t know what tomorrow holds.

But we know we have to be a regulator that moves as fast as the market does, without losing the judgement that makes us worth trusting.

And you have to be an industry that’s just as intentional. One that moves quickly where it counts, without losing sight of the people who depend on you.

          

            						

A shared responsibility

We all want a more predictable, proportionate and purposeful regulatory system.

We’ll only get there by being deliberate, with the future in mind – as this building reminds us.

So, keep telling us where the tension is, and continue engaging with the reforms already underway.

The prize is worth it: a regulatory framework that supports growth and encourages investment while protecting consumers and earning trust.

Not just for today – but for tomorrow.

title: Fraud, capital and owning the infrastructure
snippet: Discover how unified financial infrastructure and smart fraud prevention power modern platforms.
fullText:
At Money20/20 in Las Vegas, one question ran through every conversation: how do we make financial innovation work better for the people and businesses who rely on it? Here are three things that stuck with us after the discussions stopped.

Fraud is about intent, not just identity

Americans reported nearly $21 billion in internet crime losses to the FBI in 2025, up 26% from the previous year. For merchants, the daily crisis isn't one headline-grabbing technique. It's volume, sophistication, and speed, as automation turns fraud into a continuous test-and-learn cycle.

Blanket controls create problems of their own. Half of the enterprise businesses in Adyen's fraud report saw false declines rise last year, and every one is a double loss: the sale, plus the cost of acquiring a customer you then turn away.

Fraud is also concentrated: 5% of identities drive 58% of fraud value. But, while a fraudster can fake a face or a document, they can't fake years of genuine financial behavior. The answer is understanding intent across the entire customer journey, using AI to create a dynamic sliding scale between approving, asking for additional assurance, and blocking.

Platforms are best positioned to fund growth

Small businesses aren't struggling because they're failing. According to the Federal Reserve, 40% grew revenue last year and 56% expect to grow again. Yet 94% face financial challenges from uneven cash flows or credit availability, and when banks do approve a loan, 80% wait up to two weeks for funds.

As Adyen's Chief Risk and Compliance Officer, Mariëtte Swart, said on stage, "Traditional means of underwriting leave these smaller companies just invisible and underserved." Backward-looking statements miss what the software platform running a business's daily operations sees right now.

Fresha Capital serves as proof. Fresha's Chief Payments Officer, Pawel Iwanow, explained: "It's a click of a button, and the loan is approved. Why? Because of the data." One Las Vegas business used it to open a second location, and "it was all-on-platform within seconds." Today, 89% of borrowers return for a second loan.

Who owns the infrastructure matters

Most embedded finance relies on a web of partner banks. Every handoff adds complexity and delay, and when a sponsor bank changes its risk appetite, platforms inherit the disruption. 

Owning the licenses changes that. Adyen sets its own risk appetite and control framework, holds a Federal Reserve master account in the US, and connects directly to real-time payment rails, including FedNow. Payments, accounts, card issuing, and capital run on a single stack, so businesses onboard once, and the same payment data used to process daily sales underwrites financing.

For Fresha, that meant launching capital in three weeks instead of three months, without a credit team or balance sheet liability. "We as a platform don't need to be a bank; Adyen needs to be one," said Iwanow. 

The common thread

Whether the challenge is stopping fraud or funding growth, the winners will be the platforms and enterprises that own the underlying financial backend. The future isn't about slowing commerce down with higher hurdles. It's about unified infrastructure that gives teams total control over their money flows, while keeping the experience seamless for legitimate customers.

Discover how a complete financial operating system gives you the control and freedom to win the long game.

fullText:
Retail investors in the UAE moved into the companies building the physical backbone of artificial intelligence during the third quarter of 2026, while cutting their exposure to several software businesses, according to platform data from trading and investing app etoro.

Josh Gilbert, lead analyst, Asia Pacific and Middle East at etoro

The figures compare holdings among etoro’s funded UAE users on the last day of the second quarter with the last day of the third. Oracle led the list of risers, with the number of UAE users holding the stock up 86 per cent quarter on quarter. Grab Holdings followed with an 83 per cent rise, ahead of memory and storage maker Sandisk at 56 per cent.

Chip and memory names featured further down the risers list too. Broadcom ranked seventh with a 22 per cent increase and Micron Technology ninth with 20 per cent. Space companies Rocket Lab and SpaceX took fifth and sixth place, while Nike, Trade Desk and Uber completed the top ten.

Josh Gilbert, lead analyst, Asia Pacific and Middle East at etoro, said: “UAE investors are following the AI money to where it’s actually being spent, and Oracle has become one of the clearest ways to own that build-out.”

Oracle reported more than USD 30 billion in additional AI cloud contracts during its fiscal first quarter, announced in September. Gilbert pointed to Broadcom, Sandisk and Micron as evidence that investors in the region are looking beyond the best known AI names to the suppliers of the chips, memory and storage that AI workloads depend on.

Software loses ground

At the other end of the table, customer experience software company NiCE saw the largest fall, with holders down 84 per cent. Cosmetics brand e.l.f. Beauty matched that decline, and website builder Wix.com fell 77 per cent. Accenture, Salesforce and Duolingo were also among the ten biggest fallers.

“Half of the UAE’s biggest fallers sell something AI is quickly learning to do on its own, from building a website with Wix to learning a language with Duolingo, and investors in the region have stopped giving those businesses the benefit of the doubt,” Gilbert said. In his view, companies such as Salesforce, NiCE and Accenture will need to show AI as a genuine source of new revenue in their results before sentiment changes.

Consumer stocks moved in both directions. Nike rose to fourth among the risers after its shares fell to a 12-year low, while e.l.f. Beauty sat second among the fallers, which Gilbert read as investors judging individual businesses rather than the sector as a whole.

Nvidia keeps top spot

Nvidia remained the most widely held stock among etoro users in the UAE. Amazon climbed from third to second and Tesla from fourth to third, while Microsoft slipped from second to fourth. Apple, Meta and Alphabet held fifth, sixth and seventh, Alibaba moved up to eighth in place of Strategy Inc, and Nio stayed tenth.

The data covers funded accounts of etoro users in the UAE and was accurate after market close on 30 September 2026. Past performance is not an indication of future results.

fullText:
Speech by Nikhil Rathi, FCA chief executive at the Corporation of the City of London’s annual City Dinner, Mansion House.

  

Speaker: Nikhil Rathi, chief executive 

Event: Corporation of the City of London’s annual City Dinner 

Delivered: 22 October 2026 

Note: This is a drafted speech and may differ from the delivered version.

Highlights

The UK’s financial services strength provides a platform to lead the next era of technology-driven growth. 

We must move faster and focus on outcomes to protect market integrity without holding back innovation. 

The FCA will make better use of technology and intelligence and more assertive use of its powers to tackle system-wide risks and financial crime. 

Stronger partnerships between regulators, industry, government and others is essential to protect market integrity.

    

            						

The success of the UK’s financial services

In August, flight cancellations left my sons and I with an extra day in Boston.   

A Red Sox game, perhaps? No, the Rathi boys – naturally – headed straight to…the Museum of American Finance.

Funded by industry, the museum celebrates the role of finance in American life. Illuminating the powerful benefits of informed risk taking.

Three sceptical boys engrossed for nearly 2 hours. I quite enjoyed it too.

It struck me though how right George Bernard Shaw was: Britain and America are 2 countries separated by a common language.

On this side of the pond, we’re perhaps more reserved, embarrassed even, talking about why finance matters. Yet there’s plenty to cheer.

We are the world’s biggest cross-border banking, foreign exchange (FX) and derivatives trading centre. We’re second in investment management … And our commercial insurance sector has doubled in size over a decade…

A financial services sector built on trust and one the whole United Kingdom should be proud of…  

Even more so as new technologies, so many owing to our research base, transform our economy and society.

UK firms leading in:

artificial intelligence (AI) adoption and tokenisation.

consumer access to investment opportunities widened.

moving from Open Banking to Open Finance.

Lady Mayor, your myth busting campaigns have championed London and the City. Thank you for your leadership.

If we can capture this opportunity, we gain in productivity… With rewards of economic growth felt across the country.

          

            						

I say 'we' because the FCA plays an important role.

Financial services businesses and investors need confidence in markets…including their ability to withstand and recover from shocks.

That’s why ensuring the integrity of the financial services system is an FCA primary objective.

Tonight, I want to explain how we maintain it as technology accelerates exponentially. Because, while we may be getting past peak rule making, we are nowhere near peak reform or innovation. Nor past the peak intervention required to disrupt harm and support market integrity and growth.

We have seen radical technological change before… But never so widespread or disruptive. Nor combined, as now, with a new geopolitical and defence order.

The trouble is our system responds too slowly. And trust in institutions is eroded if we can’t solve problems quickly.

Regulation takes time. Legislation requires scrutiny. Parliamentary resource is precious.

Our judicial system is under immense pressure, with more litigation and weightier decisions. We risk delays becoming the norm, with legal claims written with AI’s help potentially making things worse.

We all play a part in a system that prioritises safety in process over ruthless focus on outcomes and delivery.

So, the UK finds itself in a dangerous 'innovation delta': where institutions tasked with regulating markets and the mechanisms holding us accountable lag behind.

If we maintain an analogue approach in a digital age, new products enter the market faster than we adapt… Leaving us reacting to, even overwhelmed by, changes rather than shaping conditions for the UK to thrive.

Take Meta Muse, launched 6 weeks ago, one of the fastest-downloaded apps in US history. Personal agents are profoundly changing how consumers interact with financial and health services. Such applications will reach UK consumers soon.

Frontier AI models are here, making it easier for AI agents to carry out tasks increasingly autonomously. You are fast adopters.

And rapid change in wholesale markets:

decentralised finance

24/7 trading a reality with prices increasingly forming over weekends

parallel market structures operating alongside traditional ones

Vast opportunities. But the threats to market integrity are as serious as I have seen them.

Unprecedented volatility, concentration risks, new forms of market abuse and rampant cross-border financial crime: fast-emerging technologies putting these on steroids.

Cyber security too mixes the frailties of human nature and high tech.

Our own AI minister recently said it was likely that at some point the UK’s systems will be breached. Which is why reporting and learning from near misses is so important. As is insurance for you, your customers and supply chain.

Prevention will not always work, so investment in recovery is a necessity. The gravity of the decision to press a kill switch may pale in significance with the enormity of the task to get a system running again.

In the face of all today’s challenges, the temptation is to say: 'write more rules, but do it damned well faster'.

We will, where we need to… Including aligning with any national or global AI standards, which the Prime Minister has said will be a focus of the UK’s upcoming G20 presidency.

But if policymaking is our only regulatory reflex, we’ll be stuck chasing yesterday’s market instead of embracing the one in front of us.

          

            						

Regulatory reform continues

I do not mean to suggest that we will slow down rule reform or modernisation. But our focus must be on outcomes.

We have reformed our rulebook and strengthened our operations. Capital market reforms have kicked in. 

Technology is making it easier to interact with us with reduced reporting burdens. Our widest ever range of innovation services with record demand.

And we promised less intensive supervision for those clearly trying to do the right thing, so we can focus where harm is greatest.

But the impact won’t be fully felt unless we also end tickbox compliance. Reams of potentially duplicative assurance – data packs, risk reports, internal audit. Some of these processes driven by commercial choice, others by regulation and legislation.

Sarah Pritchard, the FCA’s deputy chief executive, will engage with you to streamline unnecessary effort…. To give Boards confidence to be brave. And consider if it’s time to look again at the 3 lines of defence.

As much as 8% of banks’ workforces are dedicated to combatting crime. We should be delivering far better outcomes with those resources.

Yet we’re bogged down by excessive data collection, complex validation, and a limited ability to understand a customer’s wider context and identify risks that span borders, institutions and accounts…

As we integrate over 60,000 professional services businesses into our ambit, Johan Sekora, our new chief operating officer, who previously led Swedish banks' intelligence sharing efforts, will spearhead work to look beyond know your customer (KYC) process so we unearth actual money laundering.

Information collected through KYC, transaction and sanctions monitoring will remain valuable.

We are ready to experiment, so we can focus collective resources exactly where they are needed….

Within the FCA, too, we must continue to get better at joining up the dots. AI tools give our supervisors a richer risk picture…

…Agents can assess cases, synthesise returns and intelligence… parse millions of rows of data and identify missing or concerning information…

Freeing up our people to do the work we need experts to do: to make the hardest decisions… Such as when agentic coordination becomes market manipulation. Or judging when a risk becomes system-wide.

Expanded capability means we’ll find more risks. So, we’ll need to be open about which justify the use of resources and which don’t.

          

            						

Powers and partnership

As an institution, we have not always persuaded others of the need for legislative change… And even when we have, change has been welcome but often slow.

So: how can we do our job effectively when technology advances faster than we can write laws or rules?

The answer must be to rethink how we use powers we already have.

We have system-wide responsibilities, but a fixed view of who we explicitly regulate.

Government and Parliament decide who we authorise. This perimeter is our anchor. But we cannot let it weigh so heavily that it sinks the regulatory ship.

Today’s risks aren’t polite enough to knock on our door to introduce themselves.

Market, cyber, or criminal risks emerge from multiple networks, firms and jurisdictions….

Capital flows across sectors, regulated or not, creating complex webs of commercial incentives. And harms within our remit originating outside it. Be that mass digital harm on social media.

Insider trading on offshore gambling or prediction markets. Or outages – like Google Cloud this week – disrupting people’s access to vital services. Talk of such system-wide risks is far from academic.

Money laundering through the regulated system is not just about fraud, sanctions and tax evasion, it funds human and drugs trafficking. Their victims: society’s most vulnerable.

Parliament has provided tools to deal with such system-wide issues affecting our objectives and remit:

The Enterprise, Consumer Rights and Online Safety and Digital Market Acts to name 4.

The critical third-parties regime. An expanding anti-money-laundering remit.

It isn’t enough to ask: is this in our perimeter?

If significant harm affects markets within our remit, we should ask: what powers do we have to tackle it? Would this be a good use of resources?

The same is true of growth opportunities. Not what are they, but how can we enable them?

In every instance: who can we work with to make a difference, quickly? Because no single agency can rise to today’s challenges alone.

Working with the Met, National Crime Agency and HMRC, we’ve recently undertaken 2 of our most significant operations to disrupt suspected organised criminal gangs who seek to abuse our financial system.

So, effective partnerships are already in action:

Cooperation through the Digital Regulators Forum on Meta Muse.

A big delivery year for pensions with the Pensions Regulator and DWP.

A FCA-Bank of England roadmap on digital assets soon dovetailing with the work Chris Woolard and the industry have been doing.

And work with international counterparts.

Recent action by US authorities against anti-money laundering violations confirming the fight against financial crime remains global. 

          

            						

Call to action: we need you

We should also be open to ideas about how we can act at pace and scale.

We have seen dedicated financial services courts speed things up in other markets, for example… And the accountability system could foster collaborative working.

There are significant mechanisms to hold the FCA accountable, more than for most regulators. Appropriate given the significance of our work and the breadth of powers entrusted to us.

But accountability must be system-wide too. Whether that is to press hard on growth or engage on risks, and which are priorities and which aren’t.

Parliament is the only body that can ensure accountability across rather than within narrow remits, transcending traditional committee boundaries.

And as we significantly step up the intensity of our activity to address system-wide risks, we need you.

The earlier we can work with you – the firms we regulate and civil society – to identify emerging risks and opportunities, the faster we can give you the confidence to move.

          

            						

Close: the prize

In other words, partnership.

That is what we need now. Partnership not just between financial regulators but more widely.

Only through partnership can we deliver the system-wide response needed to protect market integrity. And that is the foundation necessary so innovation can flourish, productivity can rise and growth can endure.

The UK is incredibly well placed to harness the power of new technology. The existing strength of this sector gives us a genuine head start.

If we can harness technological progress – if we continue to lead – financial services can place the UK at the forefront of this new era of innovation.

As regulators, we are committed to creating the conditions for you to do that.

Together, we can build a future that the whole country will be proud of…

title: Verifone Moves into Merchant Financing with Commander Capital
snippet: Verifone has launched Commander Capital, a YouLend-powered financing programme for fuel and convenience retailers, repaid as a share of daily card sales. The post Verifone Moves into Merchant Financing with Commander Capital appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Payments company Verifone has moved into merchant lending with Commander Capital, a financing programme for fuel and convenience retailers powered by embedded finance provider YouLend.

The programme automatically qualifies eligible retailers on the basis of their payment volumes and store performance rather than through a rigid underwriting process. Funds can be released in as little as 24 hours, and repayment is taken automatically as a small share of daily card sales, so it rises and falls with trading.

It is a notable embedded finance step for a processor with more than 55,000 active Commander sites. Fuel and convenience retailers face volatile cash flow and large upfront costs, with fuel and merchandise inventory moving constantly and investment needs that rarely fit neatly into budget cycles.

How the financing works

Commander Capital is structured as a merchant cash advance, with YouLend providing the funding and the product connected to the retailer’s existing payment data. Verifone’s product page says operators can see an indicative offer generated from their card processing data before applying, and that funding can reach up to twice monthly card revenue.

Rather than interest, a single fixed fee applies, and the retailer chooses the share of daily card sales that goes towards repayment. On days with no sales, nothing is repaid. Funds can be used for any business purpose, from new point of sale and payment equipment to refurbishments, new locations and short-term cash flow.

The programme is open to unbranded fuel retailers and independent convenience store operators. Sites whose card processing runs through a major oil brand are directed to a separate YouLend offer.

The application itself is designed to be quick. According to the product page, it takes about five minutes, a quote typically arrives the same day, and repeat customers can draw further funding on the day they ask for it.

Payments data as a lending signal

The launch reflects a wider trend of payment processors using the transaction data they already hold to underwrite small business credit. For Verifone, it extends the Commander ecosystem used across petrol forecourts and convenience stores from payments into working capital.

Commander Capital was announced alongside a wider set of Commander product updates and new collaborations aimed at the petrol and convenience store market.

title: UK Adults Want Tax Cuts but not the Spending Cuts to Pay for Them
snippet: Taxd research finds 58 per cent of UK adults would cut council tax and half would cut VAT, but only a third would accept lower public spending to pay for it. The post UK Adults Want Tax Cuts but not the Spending Cuts to Pay for Them appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
British adults want relief on council tax and VAT, but most are unwilling to accept lower spending on public services to fund it, according to new research from tax filing platform Taxd.

Taxd‘s If I Were In Charge report asked a simple question: if you ran the Treasury, what would you change? Nearly six in ten adults (58 per cent) said they would cut council tax, against just 7 per cent who would raise it. Half (50 per cent) would cut VAT. Yet only a third (33 per cent) said they would cut taxes if it meant spending less on public services.

That gap leaves the Chancellor with a harder choice than the familiar argument over whether taxes should rise or fall, with the Budget approaching and household finances under scrutiny.

A question of fairness

Arjun Kumar, co-CEO and co-founder of Taxd

The research also points to a sense of unfairness. Some 56 per cent of respondents said the tax system is unfair to people like them, compared with 18 per cent who said it is fair. Among those who feel it is unfair, 43 per cent said tax rises had not been matched by better public services.

The findings are not simple anti-tax sentiment, however. Many respondents said they would be willing to pay more if they could see where the money goes.

Arjun Kumar, co-founder and co-CEO of Taxd, said: “What comes through is not a demand for simply more or less tax, but for a different shape of taxation: lighter on work and everyday spending, and more willing to look at wealth.”

“The same answers show the bind any Chancellor is in. Nearly six in ten adults would cut council tax and half would cut VAT, but only a third would accept lower public spending to pay for it. Every pound taken off one tax has to be found somewhere else, and an honest debate has to start there.”

Kumar is a former tax director at PwC who left to build Taxd, an HMRC-recognised self-assessment filing platform that supports more than 20,000 users.

The core data comes from a nationally representative Opinium poll of 2,050 UK adults, conducted between 9 and 11 September 2026, supported by 1,173 open responses gathered through Taxd’s public microsite.

snippet: The card network expanded its tie with the country’s largest private bank, increasing its opportunities to sell to small businesses and consumers.
fullText:
An article from
        
    

        

                

The card network expanded its tie with the country’s largest private bank, increasing its opportunities to sell to small businesses and consumers.

        

            

        Published Nov. 2, 2026
    

                        

                            

                                
                            

                

                

    
        

        

    
            
                Shoppers buy onions from a street stall at Boro Bazar on March 19, 2026, in Dhubri, Assam, India. Mastercard has been seeking to expand its reach in the country.
            
        
            Getty Images News via Getty Images
        
    
    
    

Mastercard has expanded its work with the largest bank in India, the world’s most populous country, according to comments from the card network’s CEO, Michael Miebach.

In reporting the company’s third-quarter results last week, Miebach said Mastercard had signed a small business-focused agreement with HDFC Bank during the quarter, giving the network an opportunity to sell services to the bank and potentially offer another three million cards. 

Mastercard has had a relationship with the bank since 2005, a spokesperson for the card network said by email. The company’s larger U.S. rival, Visa also has a tie to HDFC. 

The Indian bank has some 10,000 branch locations and provides services to 100 million customers, Miebach said Thursday on an earnings call.

Miebach called the business expansion an “important” development in “one of the world's most competitive markets.”

The expanded partnership comes as the Purchase, New York-based company to further its build its presence in countries around the world and increase its global market share. 

Miebach noted that the card network is cultivating relationships to reach unbanked customers in African countries like Nigeria, to cater to wealthy clients in Switzerland and to build ties in India and Brazil, where those nations’ governments have created national payment systems.

Miebach explained how the Indian government creating the UPI payment system to include more people in the country’s financial system is both a challenge to companies offering services in that country and an opportunity.

He noted news reports since August that UPI may begin to charge merchants a fee to help finance the national payments system.

“We continue to engage in India very effectively with the government, (and) with the private sector,” Miebach said, strengthening Mastercard’s debit card proposition to better compete in the market. 

UPI is bringing people “into the digital ecosystem that will graduate to different sets of products, which will include debit, and then eventually credit,” Miebach said. “There is so much opportunity in India as well as in Brazil, where we essentially pursue the same strategy.”

In both countries, Mastercard partners with companies and governments, he explained.

The company’s third-quarter U.S. gross dollar volume rose 6% over the year-earlier period to $867 billion, but a faster 8% rate to a larger $2.08 trillion outside of the U.S., according to the third-quarter presentation. Based on that third-quarter view, the business outside the U.S. makes up about 70% of the company’s volume.

Third-quarter net income climbed 18% over the year-ago period to $4.6 billion as revenue for the quarter increased 14% to $9.8 billion, according to the company’s earnings press release.

title: Birmingham Stays the UK’s Current Account Switching Capital
snippet: Birmingham led UK current account switching again in Q2 2026 with 7,748 switches, as switching among 18 to 24 year olds rose 18 per cent on the quarter. The post Birmingham Stays the UK’s Current Account Switching Capital appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
Birmingham has kept its place as the UK’s busiest location for current account switching, with 7,748 switches between April and June 2026, the latest Current Account Switch Service regional rankings show.

Newcastle upon Tyne, with 6,097 switches, and Manchester, with 6,020, completed the top three. It is the second quarter in a row that Birmingham has led the table.

Across the UK, more than 286,000 current account switches were completed in the second quarter. June was the busiest month, accounting for 115,421 switches, or more than 40 per cent of the quarter’s total.

Scotland moves up the table

Glasgow was Scotland’s leading switching location and ranked fourth across the UK with 6,005 switches. Edinburgh entered the UK top ten for the first time this year, with 4,978.

The rest of the top ten was made up of Sheffield (5,933), East London (5,575), Nottingham (5,339), Bristol (5,119) and South East London (5,050).

Younger switchers on the rise

People aged 25 to 40 remained the most active switchers, carrying out 121,251 switches, more than 42 per cent of the total and almost three times as many as those aged 18 to 24. The younger group is catching up, however: switches by 18 to 24 year olds reached 40,949 in the quarter, up by almost a fifth, or 18 per cent, on the first quarter of 2026.

The rise comes as earlier research from Pay.UK found that school leavers want a bank account that helps them budget and plan, with 29 per cent naming this, while 26 per cent said not knowing how to choose an account put them off switching.

John Dentry, product manager at Pay.UK, which owns and operates the Current Account Switch Service, said: “The latest Regional Rankings demonstrate the continued strength of competition within the UK’s banking sector, with hundreds of thousands of consumers taking advantage of the opportunity to move to an account that better meets their needs.”

He added that it was “particularly encouraging to see increasing numbers of young people switching bank accounts alongside the sustained popularity of switching among those aged 25 to 40”.

The service is free to use and completes a switch in seven working days, moving incoming and outgoing payments such as salaries and direct debits to the new account. Location figures are based on switchers’ postcodes, and Outer London areas with their own postcodes, such as Twickenham, Kingston and Harrow, are counted separately from London.
