fullText:
The UK's most innovative businesses often start small.

Before they can develop new technologies, win contracts or expand into new markets, they need access to banking services to help them operate, invest and grow.

Access to financial services can be easy to take for granted. When those services work well they're almost invisible. However, when access becomes difficult or delayed, the effects can extend far beyond a single business.

Small-to-medium sized enterprises (SMEs) operating in or providing services to the defence sector play an important role in innovation and growth.

But these businesses do more than contribute to economic growth. Many are helping to develop the technologies, expertise and capabilities that support the UK's national resilience and security.

Banking services are part of that story. They help businesses secure contracts, invest in new opportunities and grow. They are one of the key links between innovation and capability, and between economic growth and national resilience.

That's why we wanted to understand whether defence SMEs were able to access banking services efficiently and consistently.

The challenge for defence SMEs is friction and delay, not exclusion

The current debate around defence and financial services has, at times, suggested that defence businesses are routinely excluded from accessing financial services. But for everyday banking services, such as opening a bank account, the picture is a lot more nuanced.

The firms we engaged with can and do serve defence SMEs. Many are taking steps to better understand and support the sector. In some cases, they're investing in specialist expertise, dedicated teams and governance processes.

But we also heard about long onboarding processes, repeated requests for information and delays in decision-making.

The theme that emerged was friction and delay rather than widespread exclusion.

That distinction matters because it points to a different challenge. The question is not whether firms are willing to serve the sector, but whether their processes are proportionate to the risks. And whether firms can reduce friction while managing risk effectively. SMEs can also help by being prepared to explain how they manage the risks associated with their business, and by providing clear and timely information to firms.

Defence is not one-size-fits-all

There is no regulatory barrier preventing firms from supporting lawful defence businesses. Financial services firms are entitled to make commercial decisions and determine their own risk appetite. But the approach they take should be proportionate to the specific risks.

One of the strongest messages from our work is that defence should not be viewed as a single category.

The sector is vast. It includes businesses that directly support the UK's defence capabilities, as well as those that are linked through the products, services or technologies they provide including software, logistics, maintenance, engineering, manufacturing and consulting. Their activities, business models and risk profiles can differ significantly.

Whatever the business model, robust due diligence to manage financial crime and other risks remains essential. But effective risk management is also about recognising differences.

A risk-based approach should focus on the specific customer, the activities they undertake and the risks they present.

Better information leads to better decisions

Another theme that stood out was the importance of data.

Many firms told us they do not always have a clear picture of their defence customers or the outcomes those customers experience throughout their journey with the firm.

Without good information, it becomes harder for firms to answer important questions including:

Are applications taking longer than expected?

Are decisions being applied consistently?

Do governance processes reflect actual risk?

Are customers receiving outcomes that align with the firm's stated approach?

Good management information helps firms answer those questions. It supports stronger oversight, better decision-making and ultimately better customer outcomes.

Getting the balance right

Our work does not introduce new rules or requirements. But it does reinforce an important principle: firms should take risk-based and proportionate decisions based on the circumstances of individual customers, including SMEs.

When firms get that balance right, they can manage risk effectively while helping viable businesses access the services they need to invest, innovate and grow.

Ultimately, we hope this work helps firms strike that balance and ensures that businesses contributing to the UK's national resilience can access the banking services they need to succeed.

title: T+1 is a Year away and a Quarter of Firms Still have no Plan
snippet: With T+1 about a year away, Aqua Global finds 23 per cent of financial institutions have no plan, and CEO Cian Fernando warns of rushed, costly overhauls. The post T+1 is a Year away and a Quarter of Firms Still have no Plan appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
With the move to T+1 settlement about a year away, nearly a quarter of financial institutions still have no plan in place to meet the deadline, according to research from Aqua Global Solutions.

Aqua Global’s research found that 23 per cent of financial institutions have yet to put plans in place for the shorter settlement cycle, which takes effect on 11 October 2027. The transition cuts the time between a trade and its settlement to one business day, leaving far less room for manual processing and exception handling.

Cian Fernando, CEO of Aqua Global, warned that the remaining time is barely enough for banks still dependent on legacy systems, and that those who leave it late face costly overhauls.

“Readiness across the industry remains patchy. Many banks still run on legacy infrastructure that simply can’t settle trades fast enough. If they don’t modernise soon, they’ll face failed settlements, cash penalties, funding pressure and operational strain,” he said.

Late movers pay more

For Fernando, the risk lies less in the date itself than in delay. Banks that are slow to move from manual intervention to automated handling, he argued, will end up in rushed transformation programmes, reworking core processes under time pressure and regulatory scrutiny as costs and risk build.

“A year can feel like a long time. But the real pressure isn’t the deadline, it’s leaving preparations too late,” he said.

He also framed the change as an opportunity rather than only a compliance exercise. Faster settlement reduces counterparty exposure and market risk, and the automation needed to achieve it allows firms to handle higher volumes without adding headcount.

“Banks that move now will gain an edge. T+1 isn’t just a regulatory requirement, but a genuine opportunity to innovate,” Fernando said. “Early movers will be operating with confidence while their competitors are still firefighting.”

title: Elavon pursues Paze, agentic commerce
snippet: Mobile wallet Paze is “ready to do pilots,” said Wally Mlynarski, CEO of the U.S. Bank subsidiary.
fullText:
As banking and payments players grapple with the rise of artificial intelligence agents, Elavon CEO Wally Mlynarski points to two lessons that influence his agentic commerce considerations.

The first relates to fraud. Since the introduction of e-commerce, “we've been chasing and trying to stamp out fraud for 25 years, and we’ve made all the mistakes,” Mlynarski said of the industry.

That includes card verification value codes, Payment Card Industry data security standards and keyed entry transactions, all designed to manage risk, said Mlynarski, chief executive of U.S. Bank subsidiary Elavon, an Atlanta-based merchant payment services provider.

“We could go screw that up again with agentic commerce, or we can actually focus on safety and soundness,” Mlynarski said during an interview at last week’s Money20/20 conference in Las Vegas. 

Big-bank CEOs such as JPMorgan Chase’s Jamie Dimon and PNC’s Bill Demchak have expressed liability concerns with AI agents acting on behalf of customers.

The second lesson relates to costs and benefits. The mobile wallet wars of the 2010s – featuring Apple Pay, Google Pay, PayPal and, eventually, the big banks’ response, Paze – were about making the economics work, Mlynarski said. And that proved difficult. 

Wally Mlynarski

Permission granted by U.S. Bank

“Entering agents into the flow of the consumer, the merchant, the acquirer, the issuing bank, and the networks, and now trying to add economics here to make this work, or take away economics from somebody in that chain, is going to be a challenge,” Mlynarski said.  

To that end, he’s focused on understanding the value consumers are being offered, and prioritizing trust and safety and soundness, as agentic technology takes off while standards and protocols are being sorted out. 

Meta Platforms has added Stripe’s Link digital wallet to facilitate payments by its personal AI agent Muse; consumers have also started using Instinct and OpenAI’s dots. 

Such launches and pilots are “not necessarily thinking about all the safety and soundness in there,” Mlynarski said, contrasting those approaches with bank-driven efforts.

Mlynarski returned to Elavon this year after a stint at Bank of America, where he led merchant services and receivables. He said he helped shape Early Warning Services’ Paze mobile wallet, which can work within agentic commerce and address agent hallucination issues, among other things.

Paze is “ready to do pilots,” Mlynarski said. Early Warning Services is owned by seven large U.S. banks, including U.S. Bank. 

“We can create an ecosystem that does make this successful. And if we do that right and don't race into it too quickly, consumers will have a good experience. Merchants will have a good experience. Issuers will have a good experience. And then we'll see scale,” he said. 

“If we race into it and do it incorrectly,” he said, “consumers are going to be harmed.”

Mlynarski also sees his business as an accelerator for Minneapolis-based U.S. Bank’s deposits and lending growth. That includes enabling Elavon’s merchant customers to offer buy now, pay later, and providing capital for small-business clients’ liquidity needs. 

“If you think about how we position and work with our clients to bring in deposits to the bank – obviously, to keep those deposits, we have to do the full cycle,” he said. “We have to be able to do the payments portion of that, on the back end. … But if I can solve the front-end receivables side and bring in the mass volume of our retail clients or our lodging, airlines, etc., I can actually bring in deposits.” 

Weaving U.S. Bank’s capabilities and services into what Elavon offers its merchant customers is an ongoing pursuit, he indicated. 

As U.S. Bank chases growth in the small-business segment, bundling services can help the lender stand out as it seeks scale, CFO John Stern said this month. 

“More and more, my business is moving into software,” Mlynarski said. 

Clients’ point-of-sale and enterprise resource planning systems are their “lifeblood,” so “the more we can embed the bank into those solutions, we can bring lending to them when they need it, we can bring a receivables solution or other things that they might need to manage the business,” he said.

Increasingly, that includes security solutions, enabling small businesses with antivirus software, he noted. 

“We are the game of connections,” he said. “We drive all those connections together to simplify that, to package that, so the business doesn’t have to go solve that.”

title: AI agents won’t pay the way you do
snippet: Plaid’s payments head explains how payment methods might shift as artificial intelligence begins choosing how to pay.
fullText:
As agentic commerce gains wider use, the payments industry is pondering how artificial intelligence may herald a change in payment methods. 

Bots won’t be bothered by traditional payment frictions that torment humans, such as confusing checkout flows, account creation forms, password setup or poor user interfaces. 

An agent will focus on payment parameters the human consumer has provided, such as maximizing discounts or card-issuer rewards, and select the payment method it views as offering attributes that align with those guidelines, said Brian Dammeir, head of payments and financial management at Plaid. 

The San Francisco-based financial data aggregator transfers consumer account information between banks and fintechs.

As a result, it’s likely that banks, card issuers, merchants and the card networks will see shifts relative to how people pay today, he said. Dammeir discussed Plaid’s payments business and agentic transactions during an Oct. 19 interview on the sidelines of the Money20/20 financial technology conference in Las Vegas.

Editor’s note: This interview has been edited for clarity and brevity. 

PAYMENTS DIVE: How do you see the payments ecosystem changing if agents, and not humans, select a payment method?

Optional Caption

Permission granted by Plaid

BRIAN DAMMEIR: I think the main thing folks opine on, or think about, and we think a lot about this, is in an agentic world will there be different consumer preferences around payments? If, at the end of the day, you’re permissioning something to an agent, and the agent's incentive is to take the most efficient, or most effective, route to pay for the consumer they’re acting on behalf of, you could certainly see a world in which, for example, bank payments are adopted more broadly, and you could see the mix of payment methods changing in this world. That being said, I think that's all going to depend on the consumer experience and what each of those things looks like to the consumer and which appeals to them more.

Does that lead to a new world of incentives by companies to lure a bot to a particular payment option?

The opportunity here for any network payment method player is that there’s going to be a world now in which agents are talking to agents and making a decision, and representing all parties. I’ll have an agent that represents me as, let’s say, someone buying a shirt. There’s an agent on the other side representing the merchant in their best interest. Whoever is able to create technologies that allows those agents to make the best decision, hypothetically, is going to do better in the end. Now, does that then end up being like the card-centric world, the bank-payment world, or various other payment methods? Only time will tell. But that is the opportunity, right?

Will this payment decision be made at the consumer level, with humans setting those parameters, maybe choosing travel rewards or highest cash-back offers? Or will these selections rest with the agents?

The consumer really does drive behavior. Now, we as payments experts are going to know many of the idiosyncrasies of what’s going on underneath. In the card world, it’s interchange (cost), and maybe there will be these agentic standards and how they’re all talking to each other. Most consumers will not have knowledge of that, but they will understand the value they’re being given. If I tell my agent, I love flying, I love travel, I want to optimize for what’s going to give me the best there. Or maybe I’m someone who just optimizes for cash in my pocket, and I want simplicity. That’s not too dissimilar from the world today, but agents are going to be able to work through that question much more effectively than a consumer has been able to. The agent can be an expert, but the consumer doesn’t have to be. So that is what’s going to shift behavior.

What do you see in terms of agentic payments today?

Most (agents) generally have one or two wallets available. It’s early days. There’s a lot of just initial, ‘Hey, we need to get started, we need some payment methods.’ But I expect a year from now, it’s going to look very different than it does right now. It's going to be a lot more options, including, in our view, paying by bank in certain contexts.

title: Brett King’s Bank 5.0 And The Rise Of The Agentic Bank
snippet: Brett King's Bank 5.0 argues the next customer of the bank will be an AI agent. We read an advance copy ahead of its 19 November launch. The post Brett King’s Bank 5.0 And The Rise Of The Agentic Bank appeared first on The Fintech Times.
fullText:
When Brett King published Bank 2.0 in 2010, plenty of bank boardrooms dismissed as fiction his argument that banking would become something you do rather than somewhere you go. Sixteen years and several books later, that call has largely played out as he said it would. His eighth banking book, Bank 5.0: The Rise of the Agentic Bank, makes a far bigger one: the next customer of the bank may not be a human at all.

The Fintech Times has read an advance review copy ahead of the book’s global launch on 19 November 2026 at the Singapore FinTech Festival, where King delivers the Banking 5.0 keynote before a book signing with his contributing authors. Wiley publishes the global English edition and Marshall Cavendish Business the Asia edition.

The argument in one line

King states his thesis early and returns to it often: “By the middle of this century, half of all economic activity will be initiated, negotiated and executed by machines.” If he is right, the AI agents doing that work will need financial infrastructure built around them. Identity, settlement, credit decisioning and compliance were all designed for a human who signs a form, goes to sleep and waits for a reply. The back cover puts it plainly: “Those agents will need banks engineered for them. Not for us.”

Readers of the series will recognise the structure. Bank 2.0 was about self-service, Bank 3.0 about mobile and Bank 4.0 about banking everywhere. In the closing chapter King describes Bank 5.0 as something larger: “the transition from financial intermediation to economic orchestration.”

Part I: why King thinks this is inevitable

The opening five chapters make the case that AI is, in King’s words, “not overhyped; if anything, it is under-hyped”. He moves quickly from the history of automata to China’s dark factories, the labour market debate and the pace of frontier model releases, and argues that banks do not need to wait for artificial general intelligence to be disrupted. Today’s agentic tools are already enough to automate most banking workflows.

The banking experience chapter strips products back to the three utilities underneath them: storing money, moving money and accessing credit. Everything else, King argues, is a historical wrapper that generative interfaces will dissolve. “In agentic banking, the interface is the agent.”

The chapter on how fintechs “ate the banks’ lunch” is King at his most combative. He walks through each incumbent dismissal of neobanks over the past decade and uses the growth of Nubank, Revolut, WeBank and Barq to show how each one aged. On Barq, the Saudi neobank whose board he sits on, he discloses his interest. Anyone still convinced that being a solid traditional bank is enough, he warns, “will probably choke on your iced matcha latte.”

The section closes with a line that will divide bankers and regulators: “Humans will only slow down the operation of the 21st century banking industry”, King writes. A few pages later he sets out the governance model the rest of the book depends on: “humans govern objectives, boundaries and accountability; AI executes within constraints.”

A book of many voices

Bank 5.0 is not a solo effort. Nine contributing authors write or co-write chapters, and several of them are among the strongest in the book.

Dr Efi Pylarinou opens Part II by calling agentic commerce “the third rupture”, after the Silk Road and e-commerce. Her most useful observation is a blind spot she finds across the industry: “the banking industry is building infrastructure for agents as employees or co-workers. Almost nobody is building infrastructure for agents as customers.” Her account of six agent payment protocols arriving in 18 months, from Stripe and OpenAI to Visa, Mastercard, Klarna and PayPal, is a handy map of a standards race that changes month to month.

King’s own chapters on the orchestration layer and on data give the book its central technical claim: “a bank will be able to compete without a classic core banking system, but not without a data lake and foundation model strategy.” His shortlist of the main agent types (engagement, transaction, decision-making and operational) offers a practical vocabulary for any bank drawing up an architecture.

André Vellozo’s chapter on data savings is the most original in the book. Today’s agent payment stack only looks outward, treating the human as a source of funds and authority. Vellozo turns that round: the identity binding that makes an agent accountable can also make its owner a beneficiary. “A binding strong enough to assign blame is, by construction, strong enough to assign benefit.” Agent output settles into an owner-side “dWallet”, which he calls “the largest unclaimed deposit base in the history of banking.”

David G.W. Birch then makes the case for Know Your Agent with his usual wit and directness: “Without KYA, we can’t have nice things.” His conclusion that banks should provide the trust infrastructure for agentic commerce, because “AI is not by itself a defense against AI, but real cryptography is”, is the clearest strategic opening for incumbents in the book.

The tech stack, from Huawei’s vantage point

Part III is written by Jason Cao, CEO of Huawei Digital Finance, and edited by King. It is the most engineering-led section. It covers a resilience standard Cao calls the “Four Zeros” (zero downtime, zero wait, zero trust and zero touch), cloud-native cores and a real-time data layer. Cao’s distinction between the AI a customer sees and the capability the bank builds behind it is sharp: “Customer AI is the expression; Bank AI is the capability. One cannot outperform the other.” So is his argument that behavioural data, not the model, becomes the moat: “Google trains their engines on search. TikTok trains theirs on recommendations. Amazon trains on shopping behavior. What will banks train on?”

Readers should know that this is a vendor’s perspective. The headline metrics are not independently sourced, and the Chinese core migration case studies do not name the banks involved.

The half-second market

Part IV is where the book is most vivid. J.K. Khalil, formerly Division President at Mastercard, writes three chapters that turn the agentic bank from architecture into lived experience. Products give way to intent: “A mortgage is not the desire. A home is.”

His “junk drawer” passage is a good one. It inventories the value most of us leave scattered across expiring air miles, prepaid cards and forgotten wallets, and sets it against loyalty economics: “Breakage was the silent profit line.” Once agents route spending to wherever value is greatest, that line disappears. The same goes for pricing. The half-second between a customer’s yes and the confirmation screen becomes a live negotiation between customer, merchant, bank, lender and insurer agents. His message to incumbents is reassuring and pointed at once: “agents do not punish margin. They punish opacity.”

Khalil does not duck the risks. Ambient, in-context credit, he warns, “done poorly”, becomes “the most efficient predatory lending machine ever built”. On accountability he is blunt: “A bank cannot say, ‘The AI did it’.”

King’s chapter on financial inclusion raises what he calls the inclusion paradox: “AI may give every citizen access to world-class financial services while simultaneously reducing the number of citizens earning sufficient income to use them.” Jonathan Holman, CEO of Nebras Open Finance, the UAE’s national open finance operator, closes the section with a measured look at what agents built on open banking rails could mean for the bank’s ownership of the customer: “The teller fronting all financial services may return, but it might not be employed by the bank at all.”

Regulation in the rail, and some wider territory

Part V widens the lens to economics, regulation, health and organisational design. King’s regulation chapter argues that supervision has to move “into the rail”, with rules written as executable code and agents supervising agents. Some of his lines are made for conference slides (“The EU is the world’s best rule-writer and a mediocre rule-executor”). Singapore, Brazil and the UAE come out ahead of the US and Australia, because rulemaking, supervision and payments infrastructure sit closer together in those markets.

The economics chapter, co-written with Professor Richard Petty, argues that energy and grid capacity, not chips, will be the binding constraint on the agentic economy. It introduces a new readiness index that ranks China first, the UAE second and the US fifth. The authors say openly that the scores are “directional” and were built with help from AI models, and that the index is designed to be argued with. Dr Julia Michelin asks whether health is becoming a form of capital. Ross Dawson’s Human+AI framework is the most practical guidance in this part on keeping human judgment meaningful: “An approver who rubber-stamps a recommendation has added a signature, not a judgment.”

The roadmap

For bank leaders, the conclusion is the most useful part of the book. King argues that being a capable digital bank is now table stakes, and also a trap, because such a bank is “still fundamentally architected around human latency”. He puts the window to move from digital-first to agentic at two to three years: “Institutions whose AI agents are self-improving their own operations by 2029 will be uncatchable by 2035.”

He follows with a self-assessment roadmap built on five pillars: leadership and culture, technology foundations, organisational evolution, autonomous infrastructure and the agentic bank itself. A three-year transformation plan then runs across culture, technology, organisational structure and AI capability. There is a welcome dose of realism: King warns against “scorecard theater (self-scored 4s, when most banks are 1 or 2 genuinely)”.

His picture of 2050 ranks the winners as AI-native banks born after 2028, then fintechs that made the leap early, with adapted incumbents bringing up the rear, which he expects to be “the smallest representative group”.

Where readers will push back

Bank 5.0 is a deliberately provocative book, and not every reader will accept its certainty. King writes that “the destination is certain, but the journey is less so”, and some of his timelines are bold. The geography leans towards China, Singapore and the Gulf, where King now lives and advises government and industry, though he is open about those roles. Part III carries a vendor’s perspective. The later chapters stray into energy policy, climate, universal basic income and longevity, which will strike some readers as a long way from the bank balance sheet. And because the book captures a field moving month by month, some of its 2026 references will date quickly.

Chris Skinner, one of the book’s endorsers, puts this best: “You may not agree with every forecast, but that is precisely why you should read this book.”

The verdict

King has a long record of being early, and Bank 5.0 is his most ambitious book yet. It is also more of an ensemble piece than its predecessors, and the contributed chapters from Vellozo, Birch, Khalil and Holman give it depth beyond the author’s own forecasts. Bank CEOs, boards and strategy teams will get the most from it, and the closing roadmap alone justifies the time. Fintech founders building for agentic commerce will find a useful map of where incumbents are weakest.

In keeping with the subject, King is transparent about method. He used AI tools for research, planning and restyling the charts, but says that “all of the text that appears is human-generated.”

His closing line sums up the ambition of the whole series: “Banking everywhere, never with a human. Welcome to Bank 5.0.”

Bank 5.0: The Rise of the Agentic Bank launches on 19 November 2026 at the Singapore FinTech Festival. Details and pre-orders are at bank5book.com.

U.S. Bank’s Jodi Richard, chief risk officer and a vice chair, has left the Minneapolis-based lender to become chief risk officer of American Express and its national bank, effective Jan. 25, 2027, Amex said in a Thursday memo.

Troy Remington, U.S. Bank’s chief credit officer and an executive vice president, will serve as the lender’s interim risk chief while it searches for a successor, according to a Securities and Exchange Commission filing Thursday.  

Richard, who notified U.S. Bank of her departure Oct. 23, had been at the super-regional since 2014. She was appointed chief risk officer in 2018. At Amex, Richard will also become head of the global risk and compliance team and report to CEO Stephen Squeri.

The executive shuffle comes at a pivotal time for Amex, which was hit this month with a $350 million civil penalty and enforcement actions from the Federal Reserve and the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency over anti-money laundering compliance failures.

In her new role, Richard will be based in New York and join Amex’s executive committee, Squeri said. Amex’s current risk chief, Doug Tabish, will become president of enterprise shared services in February, after the current executive in that role, Denise Pickett, retires, Squeri said in a memo issued Wednesday. 

Richard’s resignation from U.S. Bank “was not due to any disagreement with the Company on any matter relating to the Company’s operations, policies or practices,” the SEC filing noted.

title: Visa adapts to tech innovations
snippet: The card network’s fiscal 2026 results show it’s reaching beyond legacy payments paths to incorporate new technologies, offer new services and extend its global reach with more partners.
fullText:
Visa is intent on demonstrating that it can adapt to a changing world, despite naysayers who earlier this year questioned whether it would be able to compete with new technologies.

In presenting the company’s fiscal full-year results Tuesday, Visa’s CEO, Ryan McInerney, rattled off a list of accomplishments for the year, including record net revenue of $46 billion that grew at the fastest rate in 15 years, excluding leaps after the COVID-19 pandemic and due to acquisitions.

All of which led to the San Francisco-based company reporting what McInerney called “milestone” results for the fiscal year 2026 that ended on Sept. 30. 

“In 2026, we also demonstrated that whenever technology changes commerce, we move with it,” McInerney said, gloating on a webcast over the results. “We anticipate what's next, and we enable its growth as the leading hyperscaler of payments globally.”

The company’s stock flagged earlier this year as analysts and investors worried that the largest U.S. card network company might not be able to adapt to technological changes, including stablecoins and agentic commerce, reshaping the payments industry. Concerns have also increased as fintech startups, such as Stripe and Adyen, gather momentum. 

But Visa’s stock soared Wednesday, crossing $400 a share for an all-time high. The increase came after Visa reported fourth-quarter net income rose 18% to $6 billion, pushing up the full-year profit 17% to $23.5 billion, according to a Tuesday press release. 

Analysts were quick to praise the financial results, with those at Bank of America citing Visa’s “broad based strength” and those at TD Cowen saying the report “demonstrated the strength of the franchise across core payments.” 

Visa’s revenue increase for the fiscal year, including a 13% jump for the fourth quarter over the year-ago period to $12 billion, occurred as the company processed 9% more transactions, 281 billion, over last year and as cross-border activity jumped 12%, McInerney said. Overall payments volume rose 9%, with 12% commercial payments volume growth outstripping consumer payment growth. 

The results showed how Visa is creating a portfolio of services beyond its traditional card payment rails. Specifically, McInerney pointed to software services sold to corporate clients increasing 19% and its value-added services consulting revenue rising 30% over fiscal 2025. Collectively, those two revenue streams made up about 40% of the company’s overall revenue.

McInerney touted Visa’s expansion by way of new partners, pointing to consulting services that include a new investment in Overwatch Data, a firm that provides threat intelligence services and its recent acquisition of fraud prevention services company Biocatch; the company’s work with Shopify and Anthropic on agentic commerce; and its support for five stablecoins and 10 blockchain projects around the world.

The company is also scaling in new regions of the world, handling its first transaction in Syria in over a decade during the year and Latin America accounting for about one-fifth of its 5.2 billion payment credentials issued worldwide. 

Tap-to-pay, tap-to-phone, peer-to-peer payments and remittances carried on its Visa Direct network are all among the ways in which Visa is seeking to keep its dominant grasp on payments around the world. 

Analysts on the webcast were particularly interested in Visa’s outlook for agentic commerce, the innovation in which shopping and payments are driven by artificial intelligence agents. While McInerney was eager to support the potential of that new technology to lift the business, he also cautioned that the agentic era is in a nascent stage, with work still being done to allow its safe and efficient use.

Some banks and online retail behemoth Amazon have made moves to block AI agents from operating on their systems.

“We want to make sure that there's a clear path to resolution in the event of a problem, so disputes, rules, and processes and things like that,” McInerney said. “And then finally, we want to make sure that this all works securely everywhere in the world for billions of users at scale.”

With consumers and businesses seeking payments security in a new era of technological innovations, McInerney contends they will reach for a brand name they know.

“As I look ahead to 2027, one thing is clear: trust is the next growth vector for Visa,” the CEO said. “Trust fuels everything we do at Visa every day, and trust will fuel our future.”

title: Brits nearly twice as likely to spot pressure tactics in horror films as investment red flags
snippet: Investors are almost twice as likely to recognise pressure tactics in a horror film as they are when those tactics are used to promote an investment opportunity, new FCA data suggests. A survey of UK 18 to 40-year-olds who own or are considering investments found 65% spotted ‘this is your only chance’ as a classic horror warning sign. But when faced with a ‘last chance to buy’ investment opportunity, only 36% said it would make them more cautious, while 37% said they would feel pressure to buy quickly or risk missing out. The pattern also holds for other pressure tactics. While 59% recognised countdowns like the ticking clock in 'Saw' as a tactic designed to make characters act rashly, just 5% said they would be suspicious of the pressure created by a rising investment price graph.Blind spots show up with novelty, too. Nearly half (47%) recognised that horror sequels often bring back familiar threats disguised as something new. Yet only 12% were similarly sceptical of a 'groundbreaking new' investment product, while 1 in 10 said being new would actually make them more likely to invest. Peer pressure and hype also influenced attitudes towards investment. While 80% recognised ‘trust me, it's fine, everyone's doing it’ as a warning sign in a horror scenario, almost 3 in 10 (29%) said excitement from friends or group chats about an investment would reassure them or make them trust the opportunity rather than doing their own research. Lucy Castledine, director of consumer investments at the FCA, said: 'Many people can spot a horror movie trap a mile off, but this survey suggests they’re far less likely to recognise the same tactics when they're used to influence investment decisions. Hype, urgency and fear of missing out can all influence how people invest, so before acting on an opportunity, do your research and make sure it's right for you.'The FCA's InvestSmart campaign helps consumers make more informed investment decisions. Its Hype Type Revealer helps people understand what may influence their decisions and how to avoid being drawn in by investment hype.Note to editors Research conducted by Attest on behalf of the FCA. Fieldwork conducted on 9 October 2026. The sample comprised 666 respondents based in the UK, and was open to all adults across the 18 to 40 age range. All participants either currently own investments or would consider buying investments in the next 12 months.Additional findings from the research include:Around half of respondents hold a stocks and shares ISA.1 in 4 own cryptocurrency.Nearly 1 in 10 own NFTs.Initial testing of the Hype Type Revealer with more than 600 retail investors found its training intervention reduced high-risk investment decisions by 34.9%, even 7 days later.

But when faced with a ‘last chance to buy’ investment opportunity, only 36% said it would make them more cautious, while 37% said they would feel pressure to buy quickly or risk missing out.  

The pattern also holds for other pressure tactics. While 59% recognised countdowns like the ticking clock in 'Saw' as a tactic designed to make characters act rashly, just 5% said they would be suspicious of the pressure created by a rising investment price graph.

Blind spots show up with novelty, too. Nearly half (47%) recognised that horror sequels often bring back familiar threats disguised as something new. Yet only 12% were similarly sceptical of a 'groundbreaking new' investment product, while 1 in 10 said being new would actually make them more likely to invest.  

Peer pressure and hype also influenced attitudes towards investment. While 80% recognised ‘trust me, it's fine, everyone's doing it’ as a warning sign in a horror scenario, almost 3 in 10 (29%) said excitement from friends or group chats about an investment would reassure them or make them trust the opportunity rather than doing their own research.  

Lucy Castledine, director of consumer investments at the FCA, said: 'Many people can spot a horror movie trap a mile off, but this survey suggests they’re far less likely to recognise the same tactics when they're used to influence investment decisions. Hype, urgency and fear of missing out can all influence how people invest, so before acting on an opportunity, do your research and make sure it's right for you.'

The FCA's InvestSmart campaign helps consumers make more informed investment decisions. Its Hype Type Revealer helps people understand what may influence their decisions and how to avoid being drawn in by investment hype.

Note to editors  

Research conducted by Attest on behalf of the FCA. Fieldwork conducted on 9 October 2026. The sample comprised 666 respondents based in the UK, and was open to all adults across the 18 to 40 age range. All participants either currently own investments or would consider buying investments in the next 12 months.

Additional findings from the research include:

Around half of respondents hold a stocks and shares ISA.

1 in 4 own cryptocurrency.

Nearly 1 in 10 own NFTs.

Initial testing of the Hype Type Revealer with more than 600 retail investors found its training intervention reduced high-risk investment decisions by 34.9%, even 7 days later.

Demands for disguised remuneration scheme loan repayments

              

  

  

  
    

        

    

      

We have seen demands being made for people to repay loans, or purported loans, provided as part of disguised remuneration schemes.

  

            						

Disguised remuneration schemes saw people – often contractors, consultants and agency workers – paid for their work through loans instead of regular salaries as a way to avoid tax. HMRC has sought to tackle this tax avoidance through what has been termed the loan charge and published guidance for those affected.

Questions have been raised about the regulatory status of these loans and whether they were ever intended to be repaid.

Some of those affected dispute liability for the amounts being claimed and challenge whether the debts can be legally enforced. If they’re unenforceable, borrowers cannot be forced to pay the money back or have any of their assets seized against the debt without a specific order.

Some consumers are, however being sent legal letters threatening potential court action and asking for immediate repayment of the loan. Repayment is being sought after these disguised remuneration loans were sold by the original provider to a third party.

Those seeking payment may ask the FCA to agree to a Validation Order. This is the formal permission needed before the loans could be enforced. We would consider any request carefully and our agreement is by no means guaranteed. If a Validation Order is required and not granted, the debt would remain unenforceable.

Anyone who receives a demand for repayment of a disguised remuneration loan, and is unsure whether they are liable for the amount claimed, should consider carefully whether to make any payment. We’d encourage them to look at the HMRC guidance and consider taking legal advice.

Consumers should not be subject to undue pressure when being contacted about a debt. If you believe you have been subjected to this type of behaviour, you should report it to us.

If you are experiencing any difficulties, whether they are health, money or other difficulties, or if you don't understand what is happening, you should raise this with those contacting you.

title: FTC, states sue Toast over fees
snippet: The agency and eight states allege that the point-of-sale services provider charges its restaurant clients and their customers hidden fees.
fullText:
The Federal Trade Commission and eight states sued Toast on Thursday, alleging that the point-of-sale company misled restaurant clients and their customers with hidden fees and subscription plans that were difficult to cancel. 

The lawsuit also said that Toast failed to deliver the customer support help that it had pledged, and obscured a 99-cent fee Toast collected from consumers who placed online orders.

“Toast failed to honor a number of its promises and instead imposed hidden fees, unauthorized charges and subscription traps that drained the hard‑earned profits of businesses just trying to serve their customers,” the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection director, Christopher Mufarrige, said Thursday in a press release.

The FTC was joined in the lawsuit by California and attorneys general in seven states: Colorado, Florida, Illinois, Iowa, Nebraska, Oklahoma and Utah.

The lawsuit, filed in U.S. District Court for Northern California, says that “at least tens of thousands of consumers have complained about these issues to the FTC, online, and directly to Toast.”

Toast said in a press release that it disagreed with the allegations “and will vigorously defend” itself against the claims.

“Toast has been cooperating fully with the FTC's review of this matter since mid-2025 and has engaged in good faith throughout, including efforts to reach a resolution short of litigation,” the company said. “The FTC disregarded the information we provided showing the extent to which our restaurant customers negotiate their contracts. We are prepared to defend our business and fight this unprecedented action through litigation.” 

Boston-based Toast sells hardware and software services, including payment processing, to help restaurants and other merchants handle their sales.

As part of their Toast agreements, restaurants must enroll in auto-renewing subscriptions, with an average cost of $900 monthly, according to the lawsuit. The monthly cost is determined by how many terminals and added services a business chooses to bundle into the subscription, the plaintiffs said.

“Toast customers frequently complain that they have been enrolled in and charged for Toast subscription add-ons without their consent,” the lawsuit says. 

Toast has “used false claims” to entice customers to enroll in subscription services, including an offer of free Toast products under some pricing plans, along with “24/7/365” customer support, according to the lawsuit.

“In fact, none of Toast’s hardware is $0, and Toast customers frequently claim that they cannot get customer support at any hour of the day,” the lawsuit said.

The company has also made it difficult for customers to end their subscriptions, according to the lawsuit.

“The convoluted, multi-step cancellation process instituted by Toast, combined with Toast’s customer support failures, prevents or makes it hard for consumers to cancel their subscriptions, saddling consumers with additional months or even years of unwanted charges,” the government plaintiffs wrote. 

The lawsuit said that Toast’s subscription cancellation process is “nonintuitive, time-consuming, far from simple, and requires the involvement and cooperation of multiple teams within Toast.”

For those who successfully ended their Toast accounts, “in many instances, Toast has hit them with unexpected high-dollar early termination fees or continued to charge them for subscription services without consent,” the lawsuit says.

The lawsuit also said that Toast is collecting obscured fees from restaurant patrons who order online.

Until July 2023, Toast collected a 99-cent fee from diners using online digital sales channels for orders above $10, beyond other fees it charged restaurants, according to the lawsuit. The company began testing this fee in some locations in September 2021, according to the lawsuit.

“Nowhere did Toast state that it, not local restaurants, would keep the fee,” the plaintiffs said. “Instead, Toast used language obscuring that it was the primary or sole beneficiary of the fee.”

The lawsuit alleges that Toast violated the FTC Act and the 2010 Restore Online Shoppers’ Confidence Act, along with the states’ consumer protection and unfair and deceptive trade practices laws.

In its press release, Toast said that no court has found that the ROSCA law applies to “negotiated business-to-business agreements, and we don’t believe it applies here.”

Toast is scheduled to report its third-quarter financial results on Tuesday.

Correction: This story has been updated to correct that Toast ended a 99-cent customer fee in July 2023.

title: Will ditching the ‘honor all cards’ rule matter?
snippet: Visa and Mastercard agreed to drop the standard in settling litigation with merchants, but the concession may not be much of a victory.
fullText:
A legal settlement ending 20 years of litigation by merchants against Visa and Mastercard includes a concession by the card networks that may not ultimately matter much.

The proposed pact, which still awaits a federal judge’s final approval, would eliminate the longstanding rule that forces merchants to agree to accept all Visa cards if they accept one, and similarly accept all Mastercards if they accept any. The rule means merchants must take the networks’ premium cards, for which they pay higher interchange fees, alongside more standard cards, including debit cards, with lower fees.

The rule change would theoretically let restaurants, retailers or other businesses accept some Visa or Mastercard cards, but not others. It would also provide more leeway for imposing surcharges when the more expensive cards are put on the counter by consumers.

But some merchants aren’t impressed. They oppose the legal settlement offered last year by lawyers for the two sides, saying the agreement falls short of expectations, and that eliminating the “honor all cards” rule would essentially be meaningless.

The CEO of American Express seems to agree with them. When Amex CEO Stephen Squeri was asked to comment on his rivals’ agreement to ditch the rule during a webcast with analysts to discuss that company’s recent third-quarter results, he said as much.

"Good luck,” was Squeri’s knee-jerk response on Friday. 

He presumably was directing that comment to merchants, who he knows would be hard-pressed to decline Visa or Mastercard cards. “It's going to be really hard, I think, for people to differentiate,” he said, suggesting there will be “consumer outrage” if merchants start rejecting certain cards.

The rule has had a somewhat equalizing effect for acceptance of cards held by elite consumers, who often pay to hold those cards and receive more benefits for doing so, and cards with fewer benefits held by consumers not interested in annual card fees. 

Amex has always been in a league of its own, with many high-income cardholder customers who are willing to pay for the privilege of receiving more perks. It’s not a party to the litigation, but Squeri’s comments are telling.

The upshot is: There's not much incentive for merchants to start discriminating between the cards they’re willing to accept. In fact, there’s a big downside, for two key reasons. 

First, as Squeri suggested, it’s a bad experience for consumers. Dan Stiel, a former card industry executive who now advises merchants on payments, shares that view. 

The last thing a retailer wants is consumers digging through their wallets in the checkout line looking for a particular card that a store clerk may or may not recognize as an acceptable card, while other customers watch and wait, explained Stiel, whose Abetica Studios firm is based in Palm Springs, California. 

“You want to create a convenient, hassle-free way to pay for your customers,” Stiel said in an interview Wednesday.

To the extent merchants make it difficult for their customers to pay, they stand to lose customers, or at least upset them. Neither one of which is good. So the idea that customers will take a liking to using one card at a particular retailer, another card at a restaurant and a third card elsewhere is a non-starter. 

The second reason merchants should be reluctant to turn away customers handing them premium cards is that those sales are typically worth their while, despite the higher fees, Stiel said.

“They are exponentially more profitable than someone who might be using a debit card,” Stiel said, describing a customer who drives into a gas station with an expensive car to buy a tank full of premium gas using an elite credit card compared to a customer with a debit card who doesn’t fill up. “It might be a lower cost for merchants, but the tickets are smaller.”

For many merchants, potentially aggravating high-end customers and losing out on bigger sales because they want to avoid higher fees would seem a short-sighted strategy. By contrast, merchants hoping to gain from a slew of smaller sales attached to lower fees might only be lucrative at extremely high volumes. 

Ultimately, elimination of the “honor all cards” rule is an “empty benefit,” Stiel said. “If the merchant community sees this as a big win, I think they’re going to find themselves deeply disappointed.”

Maybe that’s why Visa and Mastercard were willing to do away with the rule.
